title: Juwayriyyah's freed people
hook: a captive comes to ask for help with her freedom, and her marriage sets her people free (Abu Dawud)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zaynab bint Khuzaymah, whose story survives almost entirely as a name. Your line was mother of the poor.

A battle is over, and the losing tribe's people are captives. Among them is the daughter of their chief. She has made an agreement to buy her own freedom, and she can't pay it. So she does something brave: she goes straight to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to ask for help. Aisha, watching her come to the door, tells us in Abu Dawud's collection what happened next. Today: Juwayriyyah's freed people.
screen: `A CHIEF'S DAUGHTER, CAPTIVE.` → `SHE CAN'T PAY FOR HER FREEDOM.` → `SHE GOES TO ASK.`

segments.voice: The tribe was the Banu al-Mustaliq, and the woman was Juwayriyyah, daughter of their chief, al-Harith. In the report, she tells the Prophet plainly who she is, what has happened to her, and that she needs help paying for her freedom. He offers her something better: he will pay what she owes and marry her. She accepts. Then comes the part the story is really about. The news goes around the camp: the Prophet has married Juwayriyyah. And the companions, who were holding her people as captives, said, in effect: these are now the Prophet's in-laws. How can we keep his relatives as captives? And they let them go. The report counts it: through that marriage, a hundred households of the Banu al-Mustaliq were set free. Then Aisha adds a sentence of her own: she knew of no woman who was a greater blessing to her people than Juwayriyyah. One woman walked in to ask about her own freedom. Her people walked out free. Look at the chain. Her courage to ask. His answer, larger than the question. And then the companions, who weren't commanded to do anything, choosing on their own to free people because of a new family tie. Honor for one person spread outward until it became freedom for many. One more glimpse: Sahih Muslim has Juwayriyyah sitting in her place of prayer from dawn until the late morning, remembering Allah. The woman who brought freedom to a whole tribe is remembered at prayer, too.
screen: `SHE TELLS HIM WHO SHE IS.` · `HE PAYS AND MARRIES HER.` · `HOW CAN WE HOLD HIS IN-LAWS?` · `A HUNDRED HOUSEHOLDS FREED.` · then, large: `A BLESSING TO HER PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone near you carrying something they can't put down on their own: a chore that's swallowing them, an apology they're waiting for, a grudge you're holding against them, a worry nobody has helped with. Pick the one you could lift, and see yourself lifting it. If you pray, ask to be a blessing to the people around you.
Juwayriyyah, the chief's daughter who asked the Prophet for help with her freedom, and whose marriage led the companions to free a hundred households. Today's word.
Your line: a blessing to her people. One brave question, and a hundred households walked out free. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims honor Juwayriyyah bint al-Harith among the mothers of the believers, retelling from Sunan Abi Dawud how her marriage led to the freeing of her people, and many learn the words of remembrance taught to her in Sahih Muslim.

chat.says: Why did the companions free Juwayriyyah's people without being told to?
options: They were now the Prophet's in-laws, so they let them go.
They were short of food and could not feed so many captives.
The tribe had promised to convert if their people were released.
chat.meaning: When the news went around, the companions said these are now the Prophet's in-laws, and a hundred households were freed.

al-Harith.meaning: Juwayriyyah's father, chief of the tribe

Juwayriyyah.meaning: a mother of the believers, a blessing to her people

Abu Dawud.meaning: compiler of a major hadith collection
